article.title: Curl and Longevity
article.author: Britta Hedlund
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Anyone who’s had a standard lash lift and then tried a Korean lash lift usually notices the difference within a week. The curl sits differently, and it seems to hold longer than expected. Now, that’s not a marketing angle. It’s a genuine technique difference. Let’s dissect their differences so you can easily tell whether you got the right lash lift service. The Rod Shape Changes Where the Curl Sits Standard lifts typically use a rounded silicone rod that curls the whole lash evenly from base to tip. The Korean method uses a different rod. It’s flatter and has a distinct bend point. This rod lifts from closer to the root while leaving more of the length relatively straight before it curves up. That difference produces a curl that looks more like an eyeliner flick at the base, with length extending outward, even if it's not as curved as a standard lift produces. For people with naturally straight or downward lashes, lifting from the base opens the eye more noticeably than a curl that starts further along. Processing Time Gets Adjusted for Different Lashes A big part of what separates this method from a standard lift is how the perm solution’s processing time changes based on someone’s actual lash texture, instead of applying roughly the same timing to most clients. Thicker lashes need longer to hold a curl. Finer lashes need much less time, or they come out over-processed and brittle. Technicians trained specifically in this method tend to look more closely at lash thickness and existing curl pattern before deciding on timing. That closer attention is part of why the result looks more tailored to the person, rather than the same curl applied regardless of what someone’s natural lashes are like. More Care Goes Into Keeping Lashes Separated How well lashes stay separated during processing affects how evenly the curl sets across the whole lash line. Clumped or overlapping lashes during setting mean an uneven result, with some lashes curling more than others depending on how they sat during processing. Some Korean lash lift techniques put extra focus on this step. It uses finer tools and more deliberate placement to keep every lash isolated before the solution sets. That’s part of why the finished result looks more even edge to edge. Why It Tends to Last Longer A curl starting closer to the base holds its shape for longer as lashes grow out, compared to one starting partway up. As lashes grow naturally, a mid-lash curl straightens at the root first while the curled section moves further from the eye, so the lift starts looking flat sooner. A base-focused curl grows out more gracefully, since new growth extends past the curled section without flattening the visible lift straight away. Some clients report their base-lift results holding for six to eight weeks. This is longer than the four to six weeks typical of a standard lift, though this varies by individual and technician. Aftercare Still Matters No Matter the Technique There’s always the need for proper aftercare. Avoid water and steam for the first 24 to 48 hours. Skip oil-based makeup removers and don’t rub your eyes. All of it matters just as much here as with a standard lift. The technique gives a longer-lasting, more tailored result. But it only takes an instance of bad aftercare in the first couple of days to undo it all.
